extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of English literature; readers interested in Milton and the history of press censorship
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly, edited full text of John Milton's Areopagitica with an introduction and historical notes explaining the 1640s context, the 1643 Ordinance, Star Chamber regulations, and earlier forms of censorship. Useful for literary study and research into the history of printing regulation and freedom of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1643 Ordinance for Regulating Printing (Parliamentary Order)
rubrics_metrics.description: An Order of the Lords and Commons (14 June 1643) requiring that no Order or Declaration of either House be printed except by their order, and that no book, pamphlet or paper shall be printed, bound, or put to sale unless first approved and licensed by persons appointed by one or both Houses and entered in the Register Book of the Company of Stationers, the printer putting his name thereto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies procedural prerequisites for lawful printing: prior approval/licence by appointed licensers, entry in Stationers' Register, and printer's name on the work. Text includes the Ordinance's full language and context (reasoning that previous orders had been ineffective and private presses proliferated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stationers' Company registration and rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Books were to be entered in the Register Book of the Company of Stationers according to ancient custom; no person shall print or reprint works belonging to the Company or entered for a particular member without licence or consent of the Master, Wardens, and Assistants or the owner(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms Stationers' proprietary/monopoly practices: registration confers rights, reprinting requires consent of registered owner, and importation of formerly printed English books from beyond seas is restricted (forfeiture penalties). The introduction explains the Stationers' role as a customary regulatory body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorized enforcement powers and penalties for unlicensed printing
rubrics_metrics.description: Master and Wardens of the Stationers' Company, parliamentary officers and appointed examiners are authorized to search for unlicensed presses, seize presses/letters/materials, deface or render them unserviceable, seize and carry away unlicensed books to the Company's Common Hall, and apprehend authors, printers and others involved for punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinance empowers searches 'from time to time', seizure of presses and printed materials, bringing offenders before the Houses or Committee of Examinations, requiring local magistrates and officers to assist, and authorizes forced entry to overcome resistance. Penalties include forfeiture, further punishment deemed fit, and detention until restitution/satisfaction is made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Papal/Church censorship principle (Alexander VI bull & Lateran Council precedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Papal bull (Alexander VI) and later church councils required printers to consult ecclesiastical authorities and obtain special licence; works to be examined by able and 'catholic' persons, preventing anything 'wicked or scandalous, or contrary to the orthodox faith' from being printed, with harmful works to be burned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical pattern where ecclesiastical authorities (Inquisition, bishops, faculty of theology) exercised pre-publication control. The introduction cites the bull's language urging inspection by church authorities and later Lateran Council orders (1515) that no books be printed without ecclesiastical inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Star Chamber Decree (1637) restrictions on printing
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Decree of Starre-Chamber Concerning Printing' (11 July 1637) forbade printing, importing, selling or binding seditious, scismatical, or offensive books and pamphlets scandalous to religion, church, government, corporations, or particular persons, and imposed restrictions and penalties to prevent such publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The introduction quotes and references relevant clauses of the Star Chamber decree as an example of the severe pre-1644 censorship regime in England under Archbishop Laud; the decree is presented as part of the legal/regulatory backdrop that Milton opposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Milton's argument against licensing and for freedom of the press
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton contends that the press should be delivered from restraints so that 'the power of determining what was true and what was false, what ought to be published and what to be Suppressed, might no longer be entrusted to a few illiterate and illiberal individuals.' He frames free publication as an essential aspect of 'domestic' liberty and a safeguard for the republic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The introduction summarizes Milton's normative stance: licensing centralizes judgement in a few, suppresses superior thought above 'vulgar superstition', and undermines liberty. Milton's rhetoric and historical examples are cited to justify opposition to pre-publication licensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical rule: censorship expands as printing influence grows
rubrics_metrics.description: As printing multiplied and books' influence increased from the late fifteenth century onward, formal censorship institutions became more common (e.g., mandates appointing censors, ecclesiastical supervision, Inquisition involvement). Medieval immunity was due to books being of 'comparatively slight account.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The introduction traces the historical development of censorship—Berthold of Mentz (1486), Alexander VI's bull, Lateran Council (1515), French theology faculty, and Inquisition—showing the pattern that authorities instituted pre-publication controls as the printing press proliferated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural requirements for lawful printing (printer identification, lawful interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Printers must put their name on printed works; no person shall print or reprint books unless they have lawful interest in them (as entered for a Stationer or with consent of the owner), and licensed books should be entered and recorded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details appear in the Ordinance and discussion: printer's name as accountability measure, prohibition of printing without legal claim or consent, and recordkeeping in the Stationers' Register. Violations subject to seizure and punishment.
